::: {.callout-note}
**This chapter finds structure in data that has no answer column at all.**

**Assumed knowledge:** Session 5 — scaling, and why distance-based methods need it.
Session 8 — scatter plots. Session 9 — the `fit` / `predict` shape of a scikit-learn
model.

**The one idea to take away:** there is **no right answer to check against**. That
changes everything: you cannot measure accuracy, so you must justify your result instead.
This chapter is mostly about how to justify one.
:::

## 🎯 Learning outcomes {#sec-s10-outcomes}

By the end of this chapter you can:

1. Explain how unsupervised learning differs from supervised learning.
2. Describe the K-Means algorithm step by step.
3. Show why clustering must be done on scaled data.
4. Choose *k* using an elbow plot and a silhouette score, and say what to do when they
   disagree.
5. Use hierarchical clustering and DBSCAN, and say when each beats K-Means.
6. Turn clusters into a description a business can act on.

# Part A — Learning without labels {#sec-s10-a}

## 1. Unsupervised learning {#sec-s10-topic-1}

**Unsupervised learning finds structure in data that has no target column.** Nobody has
labelled anything; the algorithm has only the features.

| | Supervised (Session 9) | Unsupervised (this chapter) |
|---|---|---|
| Data | `X` **and** `y` | `X` only |
| Goal | predict `y` for new rows | find structure in `X` |
| Can you measure accuracy? | **yes** — compare to the true `y` | **no** — there is no true answer |
| Fails by | predicting badly | producing groups that mean nothing |

Three families:

| Family | Finds | Covered in |
|---|---|---|
| **Clustering** | groups of similar rows | this chapter |
| **Dimensionality reduction** | a smaller set of columns | Session 6 (PCA) |
| **Association rules** | things that occur together | Session 16 |

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — sorting the laundry"}
Nobody told you the categories. You tip the basket out and start making piles — darks,
whites, towels — because things in a pile *resemble* each other.

**Somebody else would make different piles.** By fabric, perhaps, or by owner. Neither is
wrong. **That is unsupervised learning: several defensible answers, and no marking
scheme.**
:::

## 2. What clustering is for {#sec-s10-topic-2}

**Clustering puts rows into groups so that rows in a group are more similar to each other
than to rows in other groups.**

| Use | What the clusters become |
|---|---|
| Customer segmentation | marketing groups with different offers |
| Document grouping | topics |
| Image compression | a small palette of representative colours |
| Anomaly detection | whatever does not fit any cluster |
| Exploration | the first look at data nobody has labelled |

**"Similar" means "close together" — so clustering is a distance calculation**, and every
warning from Session 5 about scale applies with full force.

# Part B — K-Means {#sec-s10-b}

## 3. How K-Means works {#sec-s10-topic-3}

**K-Means splits data into *k* groups by repeatedly moving *k* centre points until they
settle.**

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    S1["<b>1.</b> Pick k. Place k centres at random"]
    S2["<b>2.</b> Assign every point to its<br/>nearest centre"]
    S3["<b>3.</b> Move each centre to the average<br/>of the points assigned to it"]
    S4{"Did anything<br/>move?"}
    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4
    S4 -- yes --> S2
    S4 -- no --> S5["<b>Done.</b> The centres have settled"]
```

**You must choose *k* yourself.** The algorithm cannot tell you how many groups exist —
that is the whole difficulty, and Part C is about it.

### Demo 1 — watching the centres settle, step by step

```{python}
#| label: fig-s10-kmeans-steps
#| fig-cap: "Four iterations of K-Means. The crosses are the centres; watch them walk into place."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import pandas as pd

points = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_blobs.csv")[["x", "y"]].values

centres = np.array([[1., 6.], [2., 7.], [3., 6.5]])   # deliberately bad starting positions

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 3.1))
for step, ax in enumerate(axes):
    distances = np.linalg.norm(points[:, None] - centres[None], axis=2)
    labels = distances.argmin(axis=1)                       # step 2: assign
    ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], c=labels, s=12, cmap="viridis")
    ax.scatter(centres[:, 0], centres[:, 1], c="red", marker="X", s=150, edgecolor="k")
    ax.set_title(f"iteration {step}", fontsize=10); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for j in range(3):                                       # step 3: move
        if (labels == j).any():
            centres[j] = points[labels == j].mean(axis=0)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Started at:", [[1., 6.], [2., 7.], [3., 6.5]], "— all three bunched in one corner")
print("Ended at:  ", centres.round(1).tolist())
print("The true centres were [2,2], [7,3], [4,7].")
```

### Demo 2 — the same thing with scikit-learn

```{python}
#| label: fig-s10-kmeans-sklearn
#| fig-cap: "Customer segments by income and spending score, with the centres marked."
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# A real dataset: 200 mall customers, their annual income and a spending score
# the mall assigned them.
customers = pd.read_csv("datasets/Mall_Customers.csv").rename(columns={
    "Annual Income (k$)": "income", "Spending Score (1-100)": "spending_score"})
print(customers.head(3), f"\n\n{len(customers)} customers on file\n")

km = KMeans(n_clusters=5, random_state=0, n_init=10)
customers["cluster"] = km.fit_predict(customers[["income", "spending_score"]])

plt.scatter(customers["income"], customers["spending_score"],
            c=customers["cluster"], cmap="viridis", s=18)
plt.scatter(km.cluster_centers_[:, 0], km.cluster_centers_[:, 1],
            c="red", marker="X", s=220, edgecolor="k", label="centres")
plt.xlabel("Annual income (k$)"); plt.ylabel("Spending score"); plt.legend()
plt.show()

print(customers.groupby("cluster").agg(
    n=("income", "size"), avg_income=("income", "mean"), avg_spend=("spending_score", "mean")
).round(1))
```

Note `n_init=10`: K-Means starts from random positions and can settle into a poor
arrangement, so it runs ten times from different starts and keeps the best.

## 4. Scale first — always {#sec-s10-topic-4}

**K-Means measures straight-line distance. An unscaled column with big numbers decides
every cluster on its own.**

This is Session 5's lesson, and clustering is where it does the most damage — because
there is no accuracy score to warn you that the answer is wrong.

### Demo 3 — real data where the scales genuinely differ

The mall file happens to be convenient: income in thousands (range 122) and spending
score out of 100 (range 98) are already on comparable scales, so scaling would change
almost nothing. **Check before you assume you need it.**

```{python}
import pandas as pd

mall = pd.read_csv("datasets/Mall_Customers.csv").rename(columns={
    "Annual Income (k$)": "income", "Spending Score (1-100)": "spending_score"})
print("Mall file — the two columns are already comparable:")
for c in ["income", "spending_score"]:
    print(f"  {c:<15} range {mall[c].max() - mall[c].min():>10,.0f}")
```

### Demo 4 — the same file, unscaled versus scaled

A real file where the columns are **not** comparable. `loan_data_10k.csv` records
**income in rupees** (hundreds of thousands) next to **loan-to-income ratio** (a
fraction between 0 and 1).

```{python}
#| label: fig-s10-scaling
#| fig-cap: "Left: unscaled, so income alone decides and the boundaries are vertical. Right: scaled, so both columns count."
import pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

loan = (pd.read_csv("datasets/loan_data_10k.csv")
          .dropna(subset=["person_income", "loan_percent_income"])
          .sample(2_000, random_state=0))
X = loan[["person_income", "loan_percent_income"]]

print("Loan file — the two columns are not remotely comparable:")
for c in X.columns:
    print(f"  {c:<22} range {X[c].max() - X[c].min():>13,.2f}")

unscaled_labels = KMeans(4, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(X)
scaled_labels = KMeans(4, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
ax[0].scatter(X["person_income"], X["loan_percent_income"], c=unscaled_labels,
              cmap="viridis", s=6, alpha=.6)
ax[0].set_title("Unscaled — boundaries are vertical")
ax[1].scatter(X["person_income"], X["loan_percent_income"], c=scaled_labels,
              cmap="viridis", s=6, alpha=.6)
ax[1].set_title("Scaled — both columns count")
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlabel("Income (₹)"); a.set_ylabel("Loan as a share of income"); a.set_xscale("log")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

agree = pd.crosstab(unscaled_labels, scaled_labels).max(axis=1).sum() / len(X)
print(f"\nUnscaled, an income gap of ₹1,000 outweighs the entire 0-to-1 ratio scale.")
print(f"The two clusterings agree on only {agree:.0%} of applicants —")
print(f"{1 - agree:.0%} land in a completely different group depending on whether you scaled.")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Unscaled clustering produces confident nonsense"}
No error is raised. The clusters look tidy, the chart is colourful, and **43% of
applicants are in a different group** purely because of a unit choice.

**Put `StandardScaler` in front of `KMeans` unless you have checked that the columns are
already comparable** — and check by printing the ranges, as the first cell above does.
:::

# Part C — Choosing k {#sec-s10-c}

## 5. The elbow method {#sec-s10-topic-5}

**Inertia is the total squared distance from every point to its own centre.** More
clusters always means lower inertia — with one cluster per point it reaches zero — so you
cannot simply minimise it.

**The elbow method looks for the point where the improvement stops being worth it.**

### Demo 5 — the elbow on data with a known answer

`three_blobs.csv` was built from three obvious groups, so this is the easy case: the
elbow should land exactly on the true count.

```{python}
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

blobs = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_blobs.csv")[["x", "y"]].values

print(f"{'k':>3} {'inertia':>10}")
for k in range(1, 7):
    inertia = KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit(blobs).inertia_
    print(f"{k:>3} {inertia:>10.1f}")
```

**The drop from k=2 to k=3 is huge — 866 down to 121 — and every drop after that is
small.** With three genuinely separate groups, the elbow is not a judgement call; it is
obvious by eye and by number.

### Demo 6 — the elbow on real, messier data

Real customers are never this clean. Here the elbow is still visible, but it needs a
second look to place.

```{python}
#| label: fig-s10-elbow
#| fig-cap: "Inertia falls with every extra cluster. The bend at k=5 is where extra clusters stop paying."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(customers[["income", "spending_score"]])

ks = range(1, 9)
inertias = [KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit(Xs).inertia_ for k in ks]

plt.plot(ks, inertias, "o-")
plt.axvline(5, color="red", ls="--", alpha=.6)
plt.xlabel("k (number of clusters)"); plt.ylabel("inertia")
plt.title("Where does the line stop dropping steeply?")
plt.show()

print(f"{'k':>3} {'inertia':>10} {'improvement':>13}")
for i, (k, v) in enumerate(zip(ks, inertias)):
    imp = "" if i == 0 else f"{(inertias[i-1]-v)/inertias[i-1]:>12.1%}"
    print(f"{k:>3} {v:>10.1f} {imp:>13}")
```

Read the improvement column: large gains up to k=5, then much smaller ones. **That is the
elbow** — and five is the answer this well-known dataset is famous for.

## 6. The silhouette score {#sec-s10-topic-6}

**The silhouette score measures, for each point, how much closer it is to its own cluster
than to the next nearest one.** It runs from −1 to +1.

| Score | Means |
|---|---|
| **near +1** | comfortably inside its own cluster |
| **near 0** | on the boundary — could belong to either |
| **negative** | **closer to a different cluster — probably misassigned** |

Unlike inertia, it does **not** automatically improve with more clusters, so you can
compare values across different *k* directly.

### Demo 7 — silhouette across k

```{python}
#| label: fig-s10-silhouette
#| fig-cap: "Silhouette by k. Unlike inertia, higher is genuinely better, so the peak is the answer."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

ks = range(2, 9)
scores = [silhouette_score(Xs, KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(Xs)) for k in ks]

plt.plot(list(ks), scores, "o-", color="darkgreen")
best = list(ks)[int(np.argmax(scores))]
plt.axvline(best, color="red", ls="--", alpha=.6)
plt.xlabel("k"); plt.ylabel("silhouette score"); plt.title("Higher is better")
plt.show()

for k, s in zip(ks, scores):
    print(f"k = {k}: silhouette {s:.3f}{'   ← best' if k == best else ''}")
```

Both methods point at the same answer here. **They do not always.**

### Demo 8 — when the silhouette score is wrong

```{python}
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# Two interleaved crescents. The true structure is obviously 2 groups.
mo = pd.read_csv("datasets/moons.csv")
moons = mo[["x", "y"]].values
true_labels = mo["true_group"].values

for k in [2, 3, 4]:
    labels = KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons)
    print(f"k = {k}: silhouette {silhouette_score(moons, labels):.3f}")

agree = (KMeans(2, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons) == true_labels)
print(f"\nAt k=2, K-Means agrees with the true crescents for "
      f"{max(agree.mean(), 1-agree.mean()):.0%} of points.")
print("The score prefers k=2, and yet K-Means still cuts the crescents in the wrong")
print("place — because it can only draw straight boundaries. A good score does not")
print("mean a good clustering.")
```

:::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Clustering always returns clusters"}
Ask K-Means for four groups in pure random noise and you will get four groups, each with
a centre and a colour, and a chart that looks meaningful.

```{python}
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

noise = pd.read_csv("datasets/random_noise.csv")[["x", "y"]].values   # no structure at all
for k in [2, 3, 4]:
    print(f"k = {k} on pure noise: silhouette {silhouette_score(noise, KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(noise)):.3f}")
```

Those are not zero. **The elbow and the silhouette are evidence, not proof. The real
test is whether the clusters mean something to somebody who knows the business.**
::::

## 7. Profiling: turning clusters into an answer {#sec-s10-topic-7}

**A cluster number is not a deliverable.** `cluster = 2` means nothing to a marketing
team. The deliverable is a **description**.

### Demo 9 — the profile table, on its own

Before naming anything, the basic move is just a `groupby` on the cluster label —
one row of summary numbers per cluster.

```{python}
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

blobs = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_blobs.csv")
blobs["cluster"] = KMeans(3, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(blobs[["x", "y"]])

profile = blobs.groupby("cluster").agg(
    n=("x", "size"), mean_x=("x", "mean"), mean_y=("y", "mean")
).round(2)
print(profile)
```

**Three clusters, three rows, and already a description of sorts** — cluster 2 sits
near (2, 2), cluster 1 near (4, 7), cluster 0 near (7, 3). The mall data below adds the
step this one skips: turning those numbers into words a non-technical reader can act on.

### Demo 10 — from cluster numbers to named segments

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X = customers[["income", "spending_score"]]
customers["segment"] = KMeans(5, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(
    StandardScaler().fit_transform(X))

profile = customers.groupby("segment").agg(
    customers=("income", "size"),
    median_income=("income", "median"),
    median_spend=("spending_score", "median"),
).round(0)
profile["share"] = (profile["customers"] / len(customers) * 100).round(1).astype(str) + "%"
print(profile)

print("\nNow name them, and say what to do:")
overall_income = customers["income"].median()
overall_spend = customers["spending_score"].median()
for seg, row in profile.iterrows():
    rich = "high" if row["median_income"] > overall_income else "modest"
    spends = "high" if row["median_spend"] > overall_spend else "low"
    name = {("high", "high"): "Best customers — reward and retain",
            ("high", "low"):  "Untapped — money, but not spending here",
            ("modest", "low"): "Budget-conscious — low priority",
            ("modest", "high"): "Enthusiasts on a budget — grow carefully"}[(rich, spends)]
    print(f"  Segment {seg}: {name:<44} ({row['share']:>5} of customers, "
          f"${row['median_income']:,.0f}k income)")
```

**That last block is the actual output of a clustering project.** "Segment 1" became
"high income, not spending — worth a targeted offer", which somebody can act on tomorrow.

# Part D — When K-Means fails {#sec-s10-d}

## 8. Hierarchical clustering {#sec-s10-topic-8}

**Hierarchical clustering builds a tree.** It starts with every point as its own cluster
and repeatedly merges the two closest, until everything is one cluster. You then cut the
tree wherever you like.

**Its advantage over K-Means: you do not have to choose *k* in advance.** You build the
tree once and read off any number of clusters from it.

### Demo 11 — building the tree once, cutting it several ways

```{python}
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, fcluster

blobs = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_blobs.csv")[["x", "y"]].values
Z = linkage(blobs, method="ward")   # build the tree ONCE

for cut in [2, 3, 4]:
    labels = fcluster(Z, cut, criterion="maxclust")
    print(f"cutting for {cut} clusters → sizes {np.bincount(labels)[1:].tolist()}")
```

**One call to `linkage` and three different answers**, just by cutting the same tree at
a different height. Cutting for 3 recovers the true groups exactly — 60, 60, 60 — because
`three_blobs.csv` really does have three well-separated clusters.

### Demo 12 — the dendrogram, on messier real data

```{python}
#| label: fig-s10-dendro
#| fig-cap: "A dendrogram. Cutting across at a height gives that many clusters — the long vertical gap suggests where."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage, fcluster
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

sample = customers[["income", "spending_score"]].sample(40, random_state=1)
Z = linkage(StandardScaler().fit_transform(sample), method="ward")

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.4))
dendrogram(Z, no_labels=True)
plt.axhline(6, color="red", ls="--")
plt.ylabel("distance at which clusters merged")
plt.title("Cut the tree where the vertical lines are longest")
plt.show()

for cut in [2, 3, 4]:
    labels = fcluster(Z, cut, criterion="maxclust")
    print(f"cutting for {cut} clusters → sizes {np.bincount(labels)[1:].tolist()}")
```

## 9. DBSCAN {#sec-s10-topic-9}

**DBSCAN groups points that are packed closely together and labels everything else as
noise.** It has two strengths K-Means does not:

- clusters can be **any shape**, not just round blobs
- points that belong to no cluster are marked as **noise** rather than forced into one

You do not give it *k*. You give it `eps` (how close counts as "near") and `min_samples`
(how many neighbours make a dense region).

### Demo 13 — the crescents, where K-Means could not win

```{python}
#| label: fig-s10-dbscan
#| fig-cap: "K-Means cuts the crescents with a straight line. DBSCAN follows their shape."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, DBSCAN

mo = pd.read_csv("datasets/moons.csv")
moons, truth = mo[["x", "y"]].values, mo["true_group"].values

km_labels = KMeans(2, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons)
db_labels = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5).fit_predict(moons)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))
ax[0].scatter(*moons.T, c=truth, cmap="viridis", s=10);      ax[0].set_title("The truth")
ax[1].scatter(*moons.T, c=km_labels, cmap="viridis", s=10);  ax[1].set_title("K-Means")
ax[2].scatter(*moons.T, c=db_labels, cmap="viridis", s=10);  ax[2].set_title("DBSCAN")
for a in ax: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

km_acc = max((km_labels == truth).mean(), 1 - (km_labels == truth).mean())
db_acc = max((db_labels == truth).mean(), 1 - (db_labels == truth).mean())
print(f"K-Means matches the true crescents: {km_acc:.0%}")
print(f"DBSCAN  matches the true crescents: {db_acc:.0%}")
print(f"DBSCAN labelled {(db_labels == -1).sum()} points as noise (label -1)")
```

### Demo 14 — choosing between the three

```{python}
print(f"{'':<22} {'K-Means':<22} {'Hierarchical':<22} {'DBSCAN'}")
rows = [
    ("must choose k?",     "yes",                 "no — cut the tree",   "no"),
    ("cluster shapes",     "round blobs only",    "flexible",            "any shape"),
    ("handles noise",      "no — forces a group", "no",                  "yes, explicitly"),
    ("speed on big data",  "fast",                "slow (n² memory)",    "medium"),
    ("clusters of very different density", "poor", "fair",               "poor"),
    ("main use",           "the default first try","exploring structure","odd shapes, outliers"),
]
for label, a, b, c in rows:
    print(f"{label:<22} {a:<22} {b:<22} {c}")
```

# 🎯 Tasks {#sec-s10-tasks}

::: {.callout-note title="✏️ Practise"}
**Task 1 — Choose k and defend it.** For the `customers` data, produce both the elbow plot
and the silhouette curve. **State your k and give two reasons.**

**Task 2 — Prove scaling matters.** Using `datasets/loan_data_10k.csv`, cluster on
`person_income` and `credit_score` unscaled and scaled. **Report what percentage of
applicants end up in a different group.**

**Task 3 — Name the segments.** Run Demo 10 with k=4 and write a one-sentence description
and one recommended action for each segment.

**Task 4 — Cluster noise.** Generate 300 random points with no structure, run K-Means
with k=3, and plot the result. **Write one sentence on what this teaches you about
trusting a cluster chart.**
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

cust = (pd.read_csv("datasets/loan_data_10k.csv")
          .dropna(subset=["person_income", "credit_score"])
          .sample(2_000, random_state=0)[["person_income", "credit_score"]])

# Task 2 — how many applicants change group when you scale?
raw = KMeans(4, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(cust)
scl = KMeans(4, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(StandardScaler().fit_transform(cust))
best_match = pd.crosstab(raw, scl).max(axis=1).sum()
print(f"Task 2 — {1 - best_match/len(cust):.0%} of applicants land in a different group")
print("         once the data is scaled. Income is measured in hundreds of thousands and")
print("         credit score in hundreds, so unscaled, income decides everything.")

# Task 4 — clusters found in data that has none
noise = pd.read_csv("datasets/random_noise.csv")[["x", "y"]].values
lab = KMeans(3, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(noise)
print(f"\nTask 4 — K-Means split pure noise into groups of {np.bincount(lab).tolist()}.")
print("         A cluster chart always looks convincing. The chart is not the evidence.")
```
::::

# ❓ MCQs {#sec-s10-mcqs}

**Q1.** What makes clustering unsupervised?

- (a) It is less accurate.
- (b) **There is no target column, so there is no correct answer to compare against.**
- (c) It runs without training.

**Q2.** Why does inertia always fall as *k* rises?

- (a) A bug in scikit-learn.
- (b) **More centres means every point is nearer to one, until with one centre per point
  inertia is zero.**
- (c) It does not.

**Q3.** You cluster income (in rupees) and age (in years) without scaling. What happens?

- (a) Nothing important.
- (b) **Income decides every cluster, because its numbers are thousands of times larger.**
- (c) The code raises an error.

**Q4.** Your data forms two interlocking crescents. Which method?

- (a) K-Means with k=2.
- (b) **DBSCAN.**
- (c) K-Means with k=4.

**Q5.** The silhouette score for your clustering is 0.61, and the business says the
segments make no sense. What do you conclude?

- (a) The business is wrong; 0.61 is a good score.
- (b) **The clusters are mathematically separated but not meaningful — go back and change
  the features, not the score.**
- (c) Increase k until the score improves.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"}
**A1 — (b).** Which is why this chapter measures *justification* rather than accuracy.

**A2 — (b).** This is exactly why the elbow method looks for a bend rather than a
minimum.

**A3 — (b).** Demo 4 measured 43% of applicants changing group on real loan data.

**A4 — (b).** Demo 13 measured K-Means at 76% and DBSCAN at essentially perfect.

**A5 — (b).** Demo 8's noise experiment gave respectable silhouette scores on data with
no structure at all. The score cannot tell you whether a grouping is meaningful.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="✅ Before you move on"}
- [ ] I can describe the K-Means loop in three steps
- [ ] I always scale before clustering, and I know what happens if I do not
- [ ] I can read an elbow plot and a silhouette curve
- [ ] I know DBSCAN handles odd shapes and noise, and K-Means does not
- [ ] I deliver named, described segments — not cluster numbers
- [ ] **Easiest thing to forget:** clustering always returns clusters. A tidy chart is
      not evidence that groups exist.
:::
